title: Namespaces
summary: Scoping names inside one cluster: the initial namespaces, kubectl usage and DNS.

blocks.text: A namespace isolates a group of resources within a **single cluster**. Resource names must be unique within a namespace, but the same name can be used in different namespaces.

items: Each resource can be in only **one** namespace.
Namespace scoping only applies to namespaced objects such as Deployments and Services.
Cluster-wide objects such as Nodes, PersistentVolumes and StorageClasses are not in any namespace.

blocks.text: Namespaces are meant for environments with many users across multiple teams or projects. Clusters with a few to tens of users shouldn't need to think about them at all.

items: They divide cluster resources between users through **resource quota**.
Don't use separate namespaces just for slightly different versions of the same software. Use **labels** within one namespace instead.
For production clusters, consider not using the `default` namespace. Create your own instead.

rows: Lets you use a new cluster without creating a namespace first
Holds a Lease object per node; used for kubelet heartbeats
Readable by all clients, even unauthenticated. Public only by convention
Objects created by the Kubernetes system

blocks.text: Avoid creating namespaces with the `kube-` prefix. It is reserved for Kubernetes system namespaces.

kubectl get namespaces
kubectl describe namespaces <name>
kubectl create namespace <name>
kubectl delete namespaces <name>

items: A namespace is either **Active** or **Terminating**. You can't create new objects in a namespace that is Terminating.
Deleting a namespace deletes **everything** in it. Deletion is asynchronous, so the namespace shows as Terminating for a while.
`kubectl describe namespaces` shows resource quota and limit ranges, if any are set.
Namespace names must be valid DNS labels.

blocks.text: To make a namespace the default for later commands in the current context:

kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<name>
kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace:
Creating a Service creates a DNS entry of the form:

items: Using just `<service-name>` resolves to the Service in the **same** namespace. This lets the same config work in dev, staging and prod namespaces.
To reach a Service in another namespace, use the fully qualified domain name (FQDN).
Because of this, namespace names must be valid RFC 1123 DNS labels.

blocks.text: A namespace named like a public top-level domain can shadow public DNS records. Limit who can create namespaces to trusted users.

# In a namespace
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true

# Not in a namespace
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false
Namespace resources themselves are **not** in a namespace. The control plane sets an immutable label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` on every namespace; its value is the namespace's name.
In the exam, always check which namespace a task targets. Use `-n <name>` or set the context namespace before you start.

flashcards.front: Which namespace-name prefix should you avoid?
flashcards.back: `kube-`, which is reserved for Kubernetes system namespaces.

flashcards.front: Which label does the control plane put on every namespace?
flashcards.back: `kubernetes.io/metadata.name`, set to the namespace name. It is immutable.

flashcards.back: Not recommended. Use labels to tell them apart within one namespace.

questions.stem: Why must namespace names be valid RFC 1123 DNS labels?

options.text: Because the namespace name becomes part of Service DNS names

options.text: Because kubectl can't parse long names
